title: AI in Everyday Life · Episode 1
chapters: How spam filters learned to fight junk mail
How computers learned to understand speech
Why your feed seems to know you

units.t: AI in Everyday Life. Episode one.
In this episode: How spam filters learned to fight junk mail, How computers learned to understand speech, How machines learned to translate and Why your feed seems to know you.
Part one. How spam filters learned to fight junk mail.
Every day, filters quietly throw away enormous amounts of junk email before you ever see it.
Their story is one of the first great victories of everyday machine learning.
Where spam came from.

On 3 May 1978, Gary Thuerk, a marketing manager at Digital Equipment Corporation, sent a message to several hundred users of ARPANET, the network that grew into the internet, inviting them to presentations of new computers.
The network was meant for government and research use, and the reaction was swift and angry.
Thuerk later said it led to some sales, which is why unsolicited mass email never went away.
When email reached the public in the 1990s, sending a million messages cost almost nothing, so a tiny response rate could still turn a profit.
The name comes from a 1970 Monty Python sketch where Vikings chant 'Spam, Spam, Spam' until nothing else can be heard.
A 1994 case, when two lawyers advertised to thousands of Usenet groups at once, brought the word wider attention.
From rules to probability.
The first defence was a list of rules: block 'make money fast', block all capitals, block known senders.
Spammers adapted almost instantly by misspelling words, swapping letters for numbers, hiding text in images and changing addresses.
Rigid rules also caught innocent mail, such as a doctor's email mentioning a medicine name.
In 2002 the programmer Paul Graham's essay 'A Plan for Spam' popularised a filter based on Bayesian probability.
It studies emails already sorted into spam and genuine mail, and for each word works out how much more often it appears in one pile.
A new email is scored by combining its most telling words: 'winner' pushes towards spam, a colleague's name the other way.
It learns from your own mail.
You are the teacher.
Spam filtering is a classic case of supervised machine learning: learning from examples labelled with the right answer.
When you click 'report spam' or rescue a message from the junk folder, you supply those labels.
Large providers combine signals from vast numbers of users, so a scam campaign reported by early recipients can be blocked for everyone else quickly.
Modern filters look far beyond words.

They check where a message came from, how that sender has behaved before, whether links lead to known scam sites, and whether the email passes technical checks proving it came from the domain it claims, using standards called SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
The cost of mistakes.
Every filter makes two kinds of mistakes.
A false negative lets spam into your inbox, which is annoying.
A false positive sends a real message to the junk folder, which can be far worse if it is a job offer, a bill or a message from a friend.
Filters can be tuned to be stricter or more relaxed, but reducing one kind of error usually increases the other.
Most providers lean towards letting a little spam through rather than losing genuine mail.
That is why it is worth checking your junk folder occasionally, especially when you are waiting for something important, such as a booking confirmation or a password reset.
An endless arms race.
Spammers and filter builders are locked in an arms race.
As filters improved, many criminals moved to phishing, crafting emails that impersonate banks, delivery companies or government agencies to steal passwords and money.
Some now use AI to write fluent, personalised messages without the spelling mistakes that once gave scams away.
Laws help too.
Australia's Spam Act 2003, enforced by the Australian Communications and Media Authority, requires commercial messages to have consent, identify the sender and include a way to unsubscribe.
But no filter is perfect.
The best final layer is you: slow down, check the sender, and never click a link in an unexpected message asking you to log in or pay.
The key idea: Unsolicited mass messages have been profitable since 1978 because sending a million emails costs almost nothing.
Part two. How computers learned to understand speech.
Talking to a phone feels effortless now, but getting a machine to hear words took seventy years of clever engineering.
Here is how 'wreck a nice beach' became 'recognise speech'.
Why speech is hard.
Spoken words feel separate, but the sound is mostly a continuous stream with no clear gaps.
Each speech sound, or phoneme, changes shape depending on its neighbours, called coarticulation.
Accents, speed, mood, noise and microphone quality add more variation, and different phrases can sound almost identical: 'recognise speech' and 'wreck a nice beach'.
People resolve these puzzles using knowledge of language and context.
A computer starts with only a fast-changing series of air pressure measurements, sampled thousands of times a second.
A key first step is slicing the audio into tiny overlapping pieces and measuring the energy at each frequency.
Side by side, these form a spectrogram, a picture with time running left to right and pitch bottom to top.
Vowels show as bands, and 's' as high-frequency fuzz.
Templates to statistics.
In 1952 Bell Laboratories built Audrey, which recognised spoken digits from zero to nine, mostly from a voice it had been tuned for.
In 1962 IBM showed the Shoebox at the Seattle World's Fair.
It understood 16 words, including digits and commands like 'plus' and 'minus', and did simple sums.
These machines matched whole-word sound patterns against stored templates, which could never scale to everyday conversation.
In the 1970s the US defence research agency DARPA funded a speech understanding programme, and Carnegie Mellon's Harpy handled about a thousand words.
Researchers at IBM and elsewhere then championed hidden Markov models, which calculate probabilities for phonemes and for which word follows another.
With enough recorded speech, statistics beat expert rules and dominated for about three decades.
Dictation to assistants.
In 1997 Dragon Systems released Dragon NaturallySpeaking, one of the first products to let ordinary people dictate continuous speech on a home computer without pausing between words.
It needed training on your voice and a quiet room, and accuracy still frustrated many users, but it was a milestone, especially for people unable to type easily.
The next leap came around 2010 to 2012, when university and technology teams showed that deep neural networks could cut error rates substantially.
Combined with huge amounts of recorded speech and cloud computing, this made smartphone voice assistants and automatic video captions practical for millions of people.
Listening for the wake word.
A common worry is that smart speakers constantly record everything.
In normal operation they work in two stages.
A small, low-power model on the device itself listens continuously, but only for a short wake word, such as the assistant's name.
Only when it thinks it has heard that phrase does the device start recording your request and, typically, send it to powerful computers elsewhere for full recognition.
The wake word detector is deliberately simple, so it sometimes triggers by mistake on similar sounds, accidentally capturing snippets of conversation.
Most devices let you review and delete recordings and mute the microphone, which is worth knowing if privacy matters to you.
Not everyone is heard equally.
Speech systems learn from the recordings they are trained on.
If those recordings mostly feature certain accents, the systems work best for people who sound like that.

Studies have found commercial systems making noticeably more errors for some groups, including speakers of particular dialects, people with strong regional or non-native accents, children, older adults and people with speech impairments.
This matters more as voice becomes a way to access services, from banking to medical transcription.
Developers are collecting more diverse speech data and letting systems adapt to individual voices, but equal accuracy for everyone remains an unfinished job.
The key idea: Spoken words run together, vary between speakers and sound alike, so machines first turn sound into a picture called a spectrogram.
Part three. How machines learned to translate.
In 1954, researchers promised that computer translation was just a few years away.
It took more than half a century, and a complete change of approach, to get close.
Promises and rules.
In January 1954, a room-sized IBM computer in New York translated more than sixty Russian sentences into English, and organisers suggested the problem might be solved within a few years.
But the sentences were hand-picked, and the system used only about 250 words and a handful of grammar rules.
Early systems relied on such rules and dictionaries, and language defeated them.
English 'bank' can mean a riverside or a place for money, and 'it's raining cats and dogs' makes no sense word by word.
A tale of 'the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak' coming out as vodka and rotten meat is probably apocryphal.
In 1966 the United States ALPAC report judged machine translation costly and disappointing, and funding dried up.
Learning from parallel text.
By the late 1980s and 1990s, researchers, notably a team at IBM, tried something radically different.
Instead of writing rules, they fed computers documents that already existed in two languages, such as Canadian parliamentary proceedings, published in English and French.
Statistical methods worked out which words and phrases tended to correspond, and how likely each translation was in context.
This needed no grammar rules, just lots of data and clever maths.
It powered free online translators such as Google Translate from the mid-2000s.
The results were often understandable but clunky, with odd word order and meaning that drifted across long sentences.
The neural leap.
Around 2014, researchers showed that neural networks could read an entire sentence, compress its meaning into a set of numbers, then generate a new sentence in the target language.
A key improvement, called attention, let the network look back at the most relevant words of the original as it wrote each word of the translation.
By around 2016, major online services were switching to neural systems, and users noticed far more fluent results almost overnight.
In 2017, researchers introduced the transformer, a design built around attention and tested on translation.
It became the foundation of today's large language models and chatbots.
Where it still fails.
Modern translation is impressive, but it isn't magic.
Systems can produce smooth, confident sentences that are subtly wrong, which is arguably more dangerous than obvious gibberish.
They struggle with sarcasm, cultural references, wordplay and politeness levels that differ between languages.
Gender is a well-known trap.
Turkish uses a gender-neutral pronoun, and systems have been found to translate it as 'he' for doctors and 'she' for nurses, reflecting stereotypes in their training data.
Names, numbers and negatives can also be mangled.
A missing 'not' can flip the meaning of an instruction, which matters a great deal for medicine labels or legal documents.
Left behind, used wisely.
There are roughly seven thousand languages, but translation AI learns from data, and most languages have little digital text.
English, Spanish and Mandarin are well served.
Many others, including most endangered First Nations languages in Australia, have patchy or no support.
Techniques that transfer learning from related languages may help, but communities rightly expect to lead any project involving their languages.
For menus, news articles or chats with relatives, machine translation is a marvel.
Translate your text and then back again to test whether the meaning survived.
For medical information, contracts, visa paperwork or court documents, use a qualified human.
Official documents in Australia often need a NAATI-certified translator, and TIS National provides interpreters.
The key idea: Early machine translation relied on hand-written rules, which language defeated, and funding collapsed by 1966.
Part four. Why your feed seems to know you.
Every time you scroll, a recommender system is quietly running an experiment on you.
Here's how it decides what you see next, and how to take back some control.
The uncanny suggestion.
Watch one video about restoring an old timber chair, and suddenly your feed is full of sanding and staining tips.
The app didn't read your mind.
It read your behaviour.
Recommender systems are the AI tools that choose which songs, shows, posts, products and news stories you see, behind streaming, online shops, social media and dating apps.
The oldest big idea is collaborative filtering.
If thousands of people who loved the same three crime dramas as you also loved a fourth, that fourth show is a good bet.
The system asks the crowd for advice, weighted towards the part of the crowd that resembles you.
Content-based filtering looks at features of the items instead, such as genre, topic or artist.
Modern systems blend both.
The million dollar prize.
In 2006, the then DVD-rental company Netflix offered one million US dollars to anyone who could improve its movie-rating predictions by ten per cent.
It released a huge dataset of anonymised ratings, and thousands of teams around the world took up the challenge.
The prize was won in 2009 by a merged team that combined many different models into one blended prediction.
The contest became a landmark in machine learning, showing that ensembles often beat any single clever method.
It also produced a cautionary tale.
Researchers showed that some supposedly anonymous users could be re-identified by matching their ratings with public reviews elsewhere.
Recommendation data, it turned out, reveals a lot about who we are.
What the feed is chasing.
A recommender needs a target, a number it tries to push up.
For many platforms that target is some form of engagement: clicks, watch time, likes, shares, comments or return visits.
Engagement is easy to measure, and it tends to line up with advertising or subscription revenue.
But it isn't the same as satisfaction.
Think of the difference between a meal you enjoyed and a packet of chips you couldn't stop eating.
Content that provokes outrage, anxiety or curiosity can hold attention very well without leaving people better off.
Some platforms have experimented with asking users directly whether a post was worth their time, and using that as a signal too.
Which goal a company chooses shapes the whole experience of its product.
Explore, exploit and bubbles.
A system that only showed more of what you already liked would miss things you'd love.
So recommenders balance exploitation, serving the safe bet like another episode of your current show, with exploration, slipping in something new to see how you respond.
That's why one long pause on an odd video can send your feed in a new direction for days.
In 2011 the writer Eli Pariser popularised the term "filter bubble" for the worry that personalised feeds wall people off from other views.
A related fear is the rabbit hole of ever more extreme material.
The evidence is more mixed than headlines suggest: many people still meet a range of views, though some research found recommendations amplifying fringe content.
The effect depends on the platform, topic and person.
Taking back the wheel.
Lingering, rewatching and commenting all count as votes, even when you're hate-watching.
Most services let you say "not interested", hide a creator, pause your watch history or clear it entirely, and many offer a chronological or following-only feed if you go looking.
Deliberately searching for topics you want more of can retrain a feed surprisingly fast.
It also helps to remember what the system can't see: whether you felt better or worse afterwards.
Only you can judge that.
Australia's eSafety Commissioner publishes plain-language guides on managing online experiences, which are a good starting point if you want to set up feeds for yourself or for young people at home.
The key idea: Recommender systems predict what you will want next from patterns in your behaviour and in the behaviour of people like you.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did unsolicited mass email never go away?
Answer. It costs almost nothing to send in bulk.
Question two. Why is speech so hard for computers to recognise?
Answer. Words blur together and vary between speakers.
Question three. Why did early rule-based translation systems struggle?
Answer. Language is full of idioms and ambiguity.
Question four. How does collaborative filtering decide what to recommend?
Answer. It looks at what similar users went on to enjoy.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
